Landscape handbook

234 Duffy Street, Ainslie · Block 14, Section 105 · 807 m²
Everything in one place: what the site does, what it constrains, and what to build. Compiled from the surveyed base, the architect's rev E drawings, the tree management plan, the geotechnical site classification and Bureau of Meteorology design rainfall. Sections collapse and expand; the plan and the solar model are interactive.

The four things that shape every decision here. The block falls two metres from the reserve to the street, so all water moves one way, toward the house and then the street. Tree protection zones cover just over half the open back garden, so most of it cannot be dug or re-graded. The soil is free-draining sand where you want to garden and reactive clay where the house sits, which sets strict limits within a few metres of the walls. And the walking path behind the fence sits on a raised bank that holds hillside water back, which protects you most of the time but concentrates the risk into one rarer, larger event.

What to do, and when

Do now
Before the garage slab is poured
Two DN100 sleeves cast under the garage slab, one from the rear pocket and one from the courtyard, plus a spare pipe in the courtyard trench. This is the only gravity route out of the back garden and it becomes impossible afterwards.
Do now
Extend the topsoil strip to the garage footprint
The rear addition topsoil is already being kept. The garage is the bigger area at 44.9 m², and adding it takes the pile from 4 to 8.5 m³ for the same instruction. Topsoil in its own pile, under 2 m, seeded if it will sit past six months.
Do now
Agree where the stockpile, washout and vehicle turning go
Ask for the erosion and sediment control plan and pin the locations to the future paving, not the side strip. The productive strip has no tree-plan protection and compaction there cannot be undone by hand.
Do now
Add the apron and subsoil drain to the builder's scope
The ground at the addition's uphill wall is 260 mm above the floor level. About 410 mm of cut, falling 1:60 outward over at least 900 mm, with a grated channel and a subsoil drain beneath. The arborist is engaged and the hand excavation is sanctioned, so this is a scope amendment rather than a new approval.
Do now
Confirm where the subsoil drain discharges
The engineer's section F details a 100 mm agricultural pipe behind the retained edge above the addition, but no outlet is shown. It has to be piped to the stormwater via the garage sleeve, not left to soak into the ground beside the footings.
Do now
Confirm the garage roof drainage
It takes the existing house gutters as well, so 75 to 95 m² needing two or three downpipes. Confirm the fall direction, gutter position, downpipe count and that none discharges into the courtyard.
Do now
Confirm the courtyard paving level against the damp-proof course
Only 139 mm below the room floors, against the 150 mm paving normally wants. If it must go lower, that is excavation beside footings in reactive clay and the engineer should specify how.
Soon
Confirm which walls the retained edge detail applies to
Section F on sheet 05 is called up on the slab plan but the callout is hard to read on the scan. Ask the engineer to confirm the extent, and whether the edge beam retains its required embedment once the apron is cut to fall away.
Soon
Walk the reserve boundary in heavy rain
Find where water ponding behind the raised path escapes, and where it crosses the fence. Check whether the gate threshold has become the low point. Also check whether the reserve eucalypts near the fence are protected, since that would extend a protection zone across the rear boundary.
Soon
Measure the boundary fence heights
The survey does not record them and they cost the side strip about an hour of sun a day. Change the figure in the solar tool and the model recalculates.
After handover
Get the stormwater spine in
39 m along the side boundary at 1 in 19, clear of every protection zone. Native-soil backfill compacted to original density, not gravel, with clay stop-dams every 6 m on the leg nearest the house.
After handover
Shape the corner swale and the diversion bund, then mulch
Earth shaping first, then 100 mm of coarse woodchip over the woodland floor, then let a full wet season pass before planting around them.
After handover
Plant, working outward from the house
Dry-tolerant groundcovers near the paving, the lawn and fruit trees in the sunny side strip, dry-shade woodland under the trees, sedges through the swale, and the rainforest group in pots in the courtyard.

The side boundary at the vegetable strip faces east-north-east and takes the morning sun. The boundary at the garage and firepit end faces west-south-west and takes the afternoon and evening sun. Water moves in one direction across the block: off the reserve, through the back garden, past the house, to Duffy Street.

Soil

Two push-tube holes on 10 February 2026 found different profiles.

DepthBack gardenBeside the house
0 – 0.1 mSilty sand topsoil, looseSilty sand topsoil, loose
0.1 – 0.4 mGravelly clayey sand, low plasticity, dry, medium dense to dense, to 0.7 mClayey sand, low plasticity, moist, loose to medium dense
0.4 – 0.8 mSandy clay, medium to high plasticity, very stiff
0.7 – 1.1 mClayey sand, low to medium plasticity, dry, denseGravelly sandy clay, medium to high plasticity, very stiff to hard

Plasticity is the measure of how much a soil swells and shrinks as it wets and dries. Low plasticity sand barely moves; medium to high plasticity clay moves enough to lift and drop a footing. No groundwater was found and the soils were mostly dry, but temporary seepage can sit on the denser soil after rain.

The arrangement is favourable. Free-draining sand where you will plant and dig by hand; reactive clay under and beside the house where you are not gardening. Soakage and infiltration work in the back garden, the ground there is erodible and needs cover, and moisture control matters most within a few metres of the walls. Two holes is limited evidence and the transition between them will not be sharp.

Class P, and what it constrains

The site is Class P under AS 2870 for one reason, ticked on the report's own checklist: trees within the zone of influence of the building footprint. Bearing capacity is adequate and there is no fill or landslip. Characteristic ground surface movement is 20 to 40 mm, equivalent to Class M, and that figure already includes the drying effect of the trees.

Keeping the pear is the sounder choice structurally. Trees near footings draw moisture from the soil; remove one and the soil beneath slowly takes up water again and swells. Tree 2 stands about 4 m from the rear addition and the engineer's assessment assumes it stays, so removing it later would risk the ground lifting under the new slab. Retaining it keeps the assessment valid. The practical consequence is that the pear needs to come through the build in reasonable health: root pruning held to the approved minimum, arborist supervision as the plan requires, and the mulching and watering actually done.

What the engineer has designed around it

The structural drawings are issued for construction and carry the Class P classification through. Worth knowing, because several of them set limits on what the landscaping can do near the house.

Slabraft, 100 mm, SL82 top mesh, 32 MPa (changed from waffle)
Piers1 m into natural ground, maximum 2.2 m centres under load-bearing beams and pads
Edge beamsEB-1, 550 by 300, founded 400 mm minimum below natural ground
Allowable bearing pressure100 kPa, footings to undisturbed ground below the root zone
Retained edgesection F on sheet 05: reinforced block or double brick with a 100 mm agricultural pipe at its base
Excavation near footingsnote F6: no deeper than a 30 degree line from the footing edge, 45 degrees in clay
Permanent excavationnote F8: deeper than 600 mm must be retained or battered

The engineer makes the long-term maintenance your obligation, in writing. Note SV3 requires site management and maintenance in accordance with AS 2870 Appendix B and refers explicitly to the CSIRO homeowner's guide. So the paved apron, the graduated planting and the restraint on irrigation near the walls are not just prudent — they are the stated condition on which the footing design rests.

There is no stormwater or hydraulic design in the structural set, so the drainage in this handbook is the only design for it.

  • Cut deeper than 0.5 m or fill thicker than 0.4 m triggers a reassessment of the classification. The design stays inside this: the firepit is a 450 mm cut in the paved terrace, the raised lawn balances 0.12 m of cut against 0.38 m of fill, and the rear swale is formed within 100 mm of mulch.
  • Trees, gardens, landscaping and ponds can all induce abnormal soil moisture conditions near the perimeter of the structure. This governs where beds and watering go, which the planting section covers.
SunWhere the light is, season by season

Direct sunlight was modelled across the block at quarter-hour intervals, using the solar geometry for this latitude and the surveyed heights of every building and tree — including both neighbouring houses, from the ridge and eave levels recorded on their roofs, and the three boundary fences at an assumed 1.8 m. Deciduous canopies are treated as bare from 1 June to 16 September and dense outside that window, and the gum as a permanently open canopy passing 55 per cent of light — it is a brittle gum, and its canopy is thin enough that it never casts the shade its 9 m spread suggests.

AreaSummerEquinoxWinter
Rear pocket, now the utility yard7.4 h7.3 h4.5 h
Side strip, east-north-east — lawn and fruit trees8.1 h6.5 h4.0 h
Paved terrace against the house11.0 h3.9 h0.0 h
Under trees 1 and 22.9 h1.9 h1.4 h
Courtyard5.7 h3.1 h0.0 h
Back garden, average5.8 h4.4 h2.2 h
Front garden, average4.3 h3.4 h2.3 h

What the numbers mean

  • The rear pocket is the most consistently sunny part of the back garden at 7.4, 7.3 and 4.5 hours, because it sits furthest from the two-storey neighbour. It is the best winter position on the block. Its sun is strongly afternoon-weighted, five hours after noon in summer against two before, which suits the firepit.
  • The east-north-east side strip is the best summer growing ground at 8.1 hours, still workable at 4.0 in midwinter, and reasonably even through the day: about four hours either side of noon in summer, tilting to the afternoon in cooler months because the two-storey neighbour takes some of the morning. This is where the productive garden belongs.
  • The paved terrace is a summer space only — 11.0 hours in December, 3.9 at the equinox, effectively none in June.
  • Under the two trees is genuinely shaded at 1.4 to 2.9 hours, so dry-shade planting belongs there and turf will not hold.
  • The front garden is the shadier half because of the liquidambar and the two street ashes in 142 m². Sun-loving structural plants need the open gaps between canopies.
  • The two-storey neighbour and the fences matter. Together they cost between one and three hours a day. That neighbour has an eave 5.6 m and a ridge 7.1 m above the ground beside it and blocks a good deal of morning sun along that side.

Fence height is the main assumption left. The survey does not record it. At 1.8 m the fences cost the side strip about an hour a day, and each additional 300 mm costs roughly another half hour in summer. Worth measuring, then changing the figure in the tool below.

How the model works

Where the sun is

The site's position comes from the borehole coordinates in the geotechnical report, converted from the map grid to latitude and longitude: 35.25622°S, 149.15585°E. Sun altitude and bearing follow from the standard astronomical formulas — declination and equation of time from the usual series, hour angle from true solar time corrected for longitude and time zone, then altitude and bearing by spherical trigonometry. Accurate to a fraction of a degree. Times are standard time; add an hour for daylight saving, and the tool shows both.

Which way the block faces

The plan is drawn in the block's own frame with the long boundary running left to right. True north sits at a bearing of 345°39'40" from that axis, from the surveyed boundary bearings, so on screen north is to the right and slightly down. Every sun direction is rotated into this frame before use.

What blocks the light

Buildings are boxes on their surveyed footprints, with a blocking height halfway between eave and ridge levels. Trees are cylinders of canopy at the heights the survey and arborist recorded. Trees are not solid: the gum passes about 40 per cent of light year round, and the deciduous trees about 15 per cent in leaf and 72 per cent bare, switching in June and September.

The neighbours and the fences

Both adjoining houses were traced from the surveyor's drawing, with heights from the ridge and eave levels recorded on each roof. The east-north-east house has an eave at 616.54 and a ridge at 617.91, about 5.6 and 7.1 m above the ground beside it, so two storey. The west-south-west house has an eave at 614.37 and a ridge at 616.34, roughly 3.0 and 5.0 m, so single storey. The three boundary fences are modelled as solid barriers along the surveyed lines at an assumed 1.8 m. The Duffy Street frontage is left open.

The shading test

Test points sit 900 mm above ground, with ground levels from a surface fitted to the surveyed 0.25 m contours. For each point and moment the model solves exactly where the line to the sun crosses each fence plane, then walks that line in 400 mm steps out to 60 metres. Inside a building below its roof means shade; through a canopy multiplies the light by that canopy's transmission. Day totals repeat this every fifteen minutes.

What it does not account for

  • Neighbours beyond the two adjoining houses, and their sheds, garages and trees.
  • Fence heights, which are assumed rather than measured.
  • Cloud. These are clear-sky geometric hours, so use them to compare one part of the garden with another rather than as absolutes.
  • Patchiness within tree canopies, which are modelled as uniform cylinders.
  • Roof pitches, modelled as flat tops at an average height, so shadow edges are approximate by a few tenths of a metre.
  • Diffuse light, which matters most in shade. The share of visible sky was calculated separately: about 0.5 in the courtyard against 0.98 in the open garden.

Checking it

Set 21 June at solar noon and the altitude should read about 31 degrees; 21 December about 78. Both are fixed by latitude and checkable against any published table. Then compare a real shadow edge in the garden against the tool at the same date and time.

How water movesRoof, reserve and subsurface flows

Three separate flows behave differently and need different handling.

Roof water

About 242 m² of roof once the addition and garage are up. Predictable and concentrated, and it does damage when a downpipe discharges at ground level and puts a large volume into a small patch of soil beside a footing. Every downpipe positively connected to the piped system. The piped design covers it with a large margin: the two lines run at 12 and 20 per cent of capacity in the design storm.

The garage roof is the one to watch. Because the existing house gutters discharge onto it, that roof carries a combined catchment rather than its own 44.9 m² — between 75 and 95 m² depending on how much of the house drains that way, which is 3.0 to 3.7 litres a second at the standard used for sizing gutters. At roughly 47 m² per 90 mm downpipe that needs two and possibly three downpipes. It sits against the courtyard on one side and 123 mm off the boundary on the other, so confirm which way it falls, where the gutter runs, how many downpipes there are and where they discharge — none into the courtyard, all positively connected. With the house feeding it, a single blocked gutter backs up a large volume, and the overflow has to go somewhere.

Surface flow from the reserve

The raised bank does the heavy lifting. Water off the hillside collects on its uphill side and cannot cross, so it ponds and runs along the bank rather than reaching the fence. That is very likely why nobody along this row is being flooded. It also means the ground actually draining onto the fence is only the strip between the bank and the boundary, plus the bank's downhill face — a small area.

Width of the strip between bank and fenceArea1 in 10 yr1 in 100 yr
5 m106 m²1.4 L/s2.2 L/s
10 m213 m²2.9 L/s4.5 L/s
15 m320 m²4.3 L/s6.7 L/s
25 m532 m²7.2 L/s11.2 L/s

Against a corner swale carrying 294 litres a second, those are trivial. In everyday rain the drainage is heavily over-provisioned, which is no bad thing.

The bank changes the shape of the risk rather than removing it. Almost nothing arrives most of the time, and then a large volume could arrive quickly if the bank overtops at a low point or a section gives way. What is released is limited by how much water was ponded, not by rainfall. Ponding 50 m long, 15 m wide and 300 mm deep is roughly 110 cubic metres: about 170 litres a second over ten minutes, more than 300 over five.

This is why the overland flow path along the side boundary must stay open, continuous and unobstructed to the street. It carries 236 litres a second and is the thing that would handle a release of that kind. Nothing gets built across it — no shed, no raised bed, no fence, no stack of pavers.

Two further points. The runoff on the path is orange and heavily silted, so anything catching water here catches sand and fine sediment too, which is the argument for a silt sump you can shovel out. And the bank is almost certainly an ACT asset rather than yours, so report erosion, a dip forming or a rill through it through Fix My Street rather than repairing it yourself, and do not assume it will be maintained forever.

Water travelling sideways inside the soil

The back garden is loose gravelly sand from about 0.1 m down over much denser material. In sustained rain, water soaks through the sand, cannot pass the dense layer, and turns sideways downhill inside the soil. The geotechnical report calls this perched seepage, which is the term to use if you are asking the engineer about it. Two consequences. A surface diversion alone will not protect the rear addition, because part of the flow passes beneath it, so a subsoil drain is needed as well. And a gravel-backfilled pipe trench running downhill beside the house becomes a drain in its own right — the CSIRO guidance is explicit that trenches containing pipes become watercourses even when backfilled.

Risks and what stops themTen water risks, in plain terms

Ten water risks are worth setting out. They are variations on one theme: water arriving somewhere it was not meant to and either sitting there or running where it can carve a channel. Each one below covers what would actually happen, why this site is exposed to it, what you would notice, and what stops it.

RiskSeverity
Water pooling against the rear addition wallHighest
Water travelling sideways inside the soilHighest
The stormwater trench becoming a drain of its ownHighest
Downpipes discharging onto the groundHigh, easily solved
The reserve bank overtopping or giving wayRare, largest single event
Scour of the overland flow pathMedium
Watering the garden causing the house to moveMedium
Concentrated flow entering from the reserve pathMedium
The firepit holding waterLower
Mulch washing off the slopeLower
Water pooling against the rear addition wall  Highest

What happens. The ground outside the addition's uphill wall is higher than the floor inside it, by about 260 mm. Rain running down the slope arrives at that wall with nowhere to go, so it sits and soaks in. Soil that stays permanently damp against one wall while the rest of the house dries out normally makes the ground move unevenly, which shows up as cracks, doors that stick, and in the worst case damp through the wall.

Why here. The block tilts one way, about a metre of drop every nineteen metres, and the addition sits across that slope like a low dam. The floor level matches the existing house, which works everywhere except the uphill side.

What you would notice. A damp or mossy strip along the base of that wall. Water standing for hours after rain rather than minutes. Later, hairline cracks in that corner.

What stops it. Most of the answer is already in the engineer's drawings. Section F on sheet 05 details a retained edge — concrete-filled blocks or double brick, reinforced both ways on a 450 by 300 footing — with a 100 mm agricultural pipe in aggregate at its base, called up next to a suspended 120 mm Bondek slab section. That is the correct treatment for a wall with ground above floor level, and it means the uphill edge is designed as a retaining wall rather than a plain slab edge.

Three things still need settling. Where the agricultural pipe discharges is not shown anywhere, and a subsoil drain with no outlet does nothing — it must be piped, and the only route clear of the protection zones is the sleeve under the garage slab. The surface above it still wants to fall away from the wall, with a grated channel at the outer edge of the paving so surface water is intercepted before it silts up the ag drain. And confirm which walls section F applies to, since the callout is hard to read on the scanned drawing.

Water travelling sideways inside the soil  Highest

What happens. The back garden is loose gravelly sand for the first half metre, sitting on much denser material. In sustained rain, water soaks straight down through the loose layer, cannot get through the dense one, turns sideways and moves downhill inside the soil. It reappears wherever the ground is cut, which will be at the addition's footings.

Why here. The geotechnical report names this directly: temporary seepage sitting on the denser soil after rain. With twenty metres of uphill ground feeding it, there is real volume moving through that layer.

What you would notice. The wall staying damp for days after rain has stopped, when the surface nearby looks dry. Water seeping from a cut face or trench wall.

What stops it. The engineer's 100 mm agricultural pipe behind the retained edge is exactly this, so the pipe already exists in the design. What matters is that it is laid in aggregate wrapped in filter fabric, and that it is connected to the stormwater rather than left to discharge into the ground. A shaped mound on the surface will not touch this water, because it is below the surface and passes underneath.

The stormwater trench becoming a drain of its own  Highest

What happens. A trench backfilled with gravel is an easier path for water than the soil around it, so it collects water along its whole length and carries it downhill inside the trench, outside the pipe. Beside the house it delivers water along the footing line and can wash fine soil out from under the footing.

Why here. The main stormwater line runs 39 metres straight down the slope about a metre off the house. That is close to the worst possible geometry, and it is how a well-intentioned drainage job causes the problem it was meant to solve. The CSIRO guide the geotechnical report cites describes exactly this.

What you would notice. Nothing, for years. Then settlement cracking along the wall nearest the trench, or a soft spot above it.

What stops it. Tell whoever digs it: backfill with the soil that came out, compacted to its original density, not gravel or crushed rock. Where the line runs closest to the house, a plug of clay across the full trench every six metres so water cannot run its length. Keep the trench a metre off the wall wherever the layout allows.

The engineer sets the depth limit for this. Note F6 requires that a service trench near a footing must not extend below a line drawn at 30 degrees from horizontal from the footing edge, or 45 degrees in clay. With the spine about a metre out and roughly 600 mm deep against edge beams founded 400 mm below natural ground, the design sits comfortably inside that. Note F8 also requires any permanent excavation around the building deeper than 600 mm to be retained or battered, so the apron cut at about 410 mm needs neither.

Downpipes discharging onto the ground  High, easily solved

What happens. A roof concentrates an enormous volume into a few outlets. One downpipe spilling at ground level can put thousands of litres into a square metre of soil in a single storm. Beside a footing that is the fastest way to soften the ground under it.

Why here. About 242 m² of roof once the addition and garage are up, and the clay beside the house loses strength when saturated.

What you would notice. Scoured soil or a splash pit under a downpipe, and mud splashed up the wall.

What stops it. Every downpipe sealed into the pipe system, with no temporary arrangements left in place after the build. Check after the first heavy rain, and again once the builder has gone.

The reserve bank overtopping or giving way  Rare, largest single event

What happens. The raised path formation behind the fence holds water back on its uphill side in heavy rain. If it overtops at a low point or a section erodes through, whatever ponded behind it comes down at once — a concentrated flow arriving in one place for several minutes rather than a few litres a second spread along the boundary.

Why here. The bank is man-made, unlined, built of the same erodible sandy material as everything else, and carries foot traffic that keeps its surface bare. The rain photographs show water sitting on the crest rather than draining off it, which is how a low point begins.

What you would notice. Beforehand: a dip forming in the path, a rill down its downhill face, or ponding deeper and longer each wet season. Afterwards: a fan of sand inside the fence, a scoured channel, and mulch stripped off a run of the woodland floor.

What stops it. Nothing you build stops the bank failing, so stay robust to it. Keep the overland flow path along the side boundary clear and continuous to the street, permanently. Keep the diversion bund above the addition intact. Keep the firepit's rim proud of the surrounding paving. And watch the bank — if a dip or rill appears, report it through Fix My Street while it is still maintenance rather than repair.

Scour of the overland flow path  Medium

What happens. The strip along the side boundary is the designed escape route in a big storm — a shallow, wide, grassed channel. In a severe event it carries a lot of water quickly. The soil is sandy and starts washing away at roughly half the speed the design flow reaches. Bare when that happens, it deepens into a gully and stops working.

Why here. Sandy soil plus a fairly steep fall along the block. Calculated flow speed at full design flow is about a metre per second; bare sandy loam begins moving around 0.6.

What you would notice. The channel deepening and narrowing over a couple of wet seasons, sand deposited at the bottom end, grass undercut along the edges.

What stops it. Grass or thick coarse mulch over the whole length, established before it ever carries water. Rock at the top where flow enters, at bends, and anywhere the fall steepens. Never bare over winter.

Watering the garden causing the house to move  Medium

What happens. The soil beside the house is clay that swells when wet and shrinks when dry. Keeping one part constantly damp — a watered bed, a leaking tap, a timer running all summer — while the rest goes through normal cycles makes the ground rise there relative to the rest. The house is rigid and the ground is not.

Why here. The borehole beside the house found medium to high plasticity clay from 400 mm down. That is the soil that does this, and it is why the footings had to be designed by calculation rather than from a standard table.

What you would notice. Cracks that open and close with the seasons. Doors binding in one part of the year and not another. A dished or domed feel to the floor.

What stops it. Nothing planted and nothing irrigated inside the paved apron. Beyond it, plants that cope with natural rainfall, on drip you can switch off rather than a timer. Keep the thirsty, frequently watered things well away from the walls — the productive strip is four metres or more clear, which is the right distance.

Concentrated flow entering from the reserve path  Medium

What happens. The walking path outside the fence is worn to bare earth and slightly incised, so it collects sheet flow from upslope and carries it along the boundary until it finds a low point. Then all of it enters in one place, with enough force to cut a groove.

Why here. The photographs show the path, along with logs laid across the slope and heavy mulching — erosion-control works, so somebody has already concluded this ground moves water.

What you would notice. A fan of silt or leaf litter just inside the fence at one spot, a scoured line running from it into the garden, or the gate threshold washing out.

What stops it. Find the low point in heavy rain, bring the swale across to meet it, and armour that entry with rock so incoming flow spreads instead of cutting in. Make sure the gate is not the low point.

The firepit holding water  Lower

What happens. A 450 mm hole on a sloping site can collect water from uphill and hold it, because its floor is below the surrounding ground. You end up bailing it out before you can use it.

Why here. Less of a problem than it sounds. It sits in the paved terrace at the low end of the garden, in free-draining sandy ground, with no sheet flow crossing it — the overland route runs down the far side of the block.

What you would notice. Water sitting in it for a day or two after heavy rain.

What stops it. A base of coarse gravel rather than compacted soil or a sealed floor. A raised lip on the uphill side, 50 to 100 mm above the surrounding paving. A small gravel-filled soak pit beside it rather than a pipe connection.

Mulch washing off the slope  Lower

What happens. The tree plan requires 100 mm of woodchip over the root zones and the planting depends on it. On a slope, fine mulch floats and moves in the first heavy rain, banking up at the bottom and leaving bare soil where you need cover.

Why here. A one-in-nineteen fall across the whole area that needs mulching, over erodible sandy soil.

What you would notice. Mulch piled against the lower fence or paving edge, bare patches uphill, and mulch in the swale where it blocks things.

What stops it. Coarse grade chip, around 25 mm, not fine or shredded — coarse chip knits together and stays put. Lines of logs or rock across the slope in the steeper pockets, the same technique already used in the reserve.

FireWhat backing onto the reserve means, and the three things sitting too close

The rear boundary is the edge of Mount Ainslie Nature Reserve — 637 hectares of yellow box and Blakely's red gum grassy woodland, rising about 230 metres from this block to the summit, with mature eucalypts standing within a few metres of the fence on the reserve side. That is the exposure, and the block is inside the ACT's mapped bushfire prone area. The construction side of that is settled with the certifier, so what is left is the garden — where the honest answer is that the layout is mostly fine and three specific things are not.

Garage11.8 m
Existing house16.4 m

The block falls 2.08 m from that boundary to the street, about 1 in 19, or three degrees, and the reserve climbs away behind it. So the reserve side is the high side, which cuts both ways. Fire arriving from the reserve is running downslope for its last stretch, the slower and less intense direction. But anything that gets loose in the garden is travelling uphill into the reserve, the fast direction — which is the argument for keeping the fire down at the house end rather than up against the fence.

Embers, not a wall of flame

Houses at an interface like this are mostly lost to embers, not to flame contact or radiant heat. Embers travel ahead of a fire, land in gutters, against walls, under decks and in fine dry material, and start small fires that are unattended because everyone is watching the horizon. Radiant heat matters at short range: the ACT standards size protection zones so that buildings are not exposed to more than 29 kW/m². At 5.9 m the rear addition is close enough that the fuel in the last few metres genuinely counts, which is what the rest of this section is about.

Scale this correctly. Mount Ainslie is an isolated grassy woodland hill, not the forested country west of Canberra that drove the 2003 fires. The realistic case here is a grass and woodland fire on the hill with ember attack ahead of it, over in hours rather than days. That is a serious event to be ready for, not a firestorm.

The block is inside the mapped bushfire prone area

ACTmapi's bushfire map returns this block — Canberra Central Ainslie, Section 105, Block 14, 234 Duffy Street, 807 m² — inside the mapped area. The whole block is within it, the mapping continues several blocks further into the suburb, and the deeper tone over the reserve is the fire management zoning laid over the hazard itself. It is not a marginal call, and it is not bad luck: the strategic plan defines bushfire prone areas as the built-up parts of Canberra adjacent to forest and grassland, which is a description of this street.

Three ACT terms get used interchangeably and are not the same thing. A bushfire prone area is the mapping that matters here — built-up land next to forest or grassland, assessed as high risk to life and property, and the thing that triggers the construction standard. The bushfire abatement zone is a separate declaration under the Emergencies Act covering rural land west of Canberra toward the Murrumbidgee, and does not apply on this side of the city. Fire management zones are the fuel management layer, reviewed annually against the urban edge, and they govern what the reserve managers do behind the fence rather than what you do inside it.

The consequence of the listing falls on the building rather than the garden: work on a bushfire prone block has to meet AS 3959, at a bushfire attack level taken from the Territory Plan precinct map and code, or otherwise from the Building Act. That is resolved and the certifier is satisfied, so it needs nothing further from you.

It does leave one thread into the garden. An attack level is calculated from the classified vegetation, the distance to it and the slope beneath it, so the assessment will have assumed something about what stands in the last few metres of the back garden. Worth knowing what, before you plant the rear screen — not because it is likely to be a problem, but because a screen is the one thing you could plant that changes an input to it.

Two things sit too close

The firepit is not one of them. It sits in the paved terrace against the house, 15.8 m from the reserve, with a non-combustible surround in every direction — which is the only place on this block where the three metre clearance rule is comfortably met, and it puts the fire where people actually sit.

The shed at the rear corner. At 0.7 m from the boundary it is the first thing embers reach, and a shed that catches will radiate onto whatever is behind it for as long as it burns. A shed there is not wrong, but it should be the non-combustible one and it should hold the tools rather than the firewood.

The ladder under the gum. Tree 1 is a 15 m brittle gum two metres inside the boundary, and the planting plan puts a shrub layer and 100 mm of mulch beneath it. Vegetation between the ground and about two metres is what lets a ground fire climb into a canopy, and a canopy fire two metres from the fence is a different problem from a grass fire. Keep that layer broken up rather than continuous.

The firepit, legally

Open air fires are prohibited in the ACT under the Environment Protection Regulation, with an exemption for fires used for cooking or heating in a container that will hold the fire. A properly built sunken firepit qualifies. Four things go with it.

RuleWhat it means here
Three metres clear of anything that burnsMet in the paved terrace, in every direction
Constant adult supervision, and a way to put it outA charged hose that reaches the rear corner, not a bucket
Seasoned firewood onlyBurning green or wet wood is a separate offence, and the smoke is a nuisance duty as well
Nothing at all during a total fire banWood fires and firepits are banned outright. Gas stays legal, supervised and clear

The declared bushfire season runs 1 October to 31 March, and shifts with the season. Total fire bans are declared on top of it, day by day. For a built-up block a permit is not normally needed outside a ban, but ACT Fire & Rescue will confirm for this address on 02 6207 8472.

Mulch and planting, against the drainage design

There is a genuine conflict here and it should be stated rather than smoothed over. The drainage design needs 100 mm of coarse woodchip across the woodland floor at the reserve end, and that mulch blanket reaches within 0.3 m of the boundary. In fire terms it is fuel at the interface. Three things make it defensible.

  • It is coarse, not fine. The mulch that causes trouble is fine, shredded or stringy material that lights from an ember and creeps. Coarse chip at around 25 mm is much harder to ignite and does not carry fire well, and it is already specified that way for a different reason — fine mulch floats.
  • It is nowhere near a wall. The nearest building is 5.9 m away, and the planting plan already puts 0.9 m of paving right around the house with no beds and nothing planted in it, for footing reasons. The dangerous case is mulch banked against cladding, which does not arise.
  • It is damp for the half of the year that matters least, and bare for the half that matters most. This is the weak point. Through summer the blanket is dry, so the mulch depth needs checking before each season rather than only being topped up when it looks thin.

The planting follows the same logic. The acacia and hakea screen along the rear gives the filtered privacy from the walking track and matches the reserve revegetation, but a continuous unbroken screen along the boundary is also a continuous fuel path. Break it into runs with the gravel path and the lawn, keep the shrubs clear of the gum's trunk, and keep dead material out of them — fine dead twiggy growth inside a shrub is the most ignitable thing in a garden. The dichondra lawn earns its place here: a maintained, watered lawn is a break, and it sits between the woodland end and the paving.

What the layout already gets right. The paved apron and terrace against the house are non-combustible and continuous, which is the single best ember defence a garden can offer. Moving in from the reserve you cross the woodland, then the lawn, then the paving before reaching a wall, which is the right order. And the water tank sits at the rear where it is useful, so long as its outlet takes a standard hose fitting.

What to do

  1. Before the firepit is built, move it about three metres toward the street and confirm the new position in the plan tool.
  2. Run a hose line to the rear corner that reaches the firepit and the rear fence, and keep a fitting on the tank.
  3. Each September, before the season: check the mulch depth, clear dead material out of the rear screen, cut back anything that has grown into a ladder under the gum, and clear the gutters. Clearing the courtyard grate is already an autumn job; this is the same walk around the house, done before summer instead of after it.
  4. Write the survival plan. It decides in advance whether you leave early, and on which rating. The ACT Emergency Services Agency publishes a template. This is the part that actually matters and the part most people skip.

This section is a design review against published guidance, not a bushfire attack level assessment. A BAL is set by a formal method under AS 3959 using the vegetation classification, the slope beneath that vegetation and the fire weather index, and only a qualified assessor can issue one. The block is inside the mapped area and that assessment has been done; where it and this section differ, it governs.

Trees and approvalsWhat the tree plan permits inside a protection zone

Five protected trees were assessed. Hand excavation around the pear is approved and under way with the arborist's sign-off, so it is worth setting out precisely what is allowed inside a protection zone, because the general notes on the tree protection drawing read more restrictively than the clauses behind them.

ActivityWhat the plan requiresClause
Excavation generallyAnything deeper than 50 mm counts as excavation. Only excavations shown on the approved plan are permitted, and the method must be hand digging, hydro-excavation or under-boring6.2.1, 6.2.2, 6.2.4
Root limitsNo root over 30 mm diameter may be cut. A non-destructive locating trench must be dug along the line of excavation nearest the tree before any site cut6.2.7, 6.3.3
SupervisionAll groundwork in trees 1 and 2's zones under a qualified arborist, AQF Cert V or above6.3.2
ServicesThrough a zone only by hydro or hand excavation, or bored beneath at a minimum depth of 1,000 mm. No additional services through a zone unless specified in the plan6.5.1, 6.5.2
LandscapingAll landscaping inside a zone under arborist supervision. Paths and garden beds must be built above existing grade with no excavation and no compaction. Planting holes hand-dug6.6.2, 6.6.3, 6.6.4
Trafficable surfacesGround protection: rumble boards over 200 mm of 25 mm coarse woodchip, cellular geotextile, or rated protection mats5.10.3
  • The apron and subsoil drain at the addition's uphill wall are achievable now, using the same method, tree and supervision as the footing excavation already approved. They need adding to the approved scope, and belong in the builder's works rather than the later landscaping, because they are building perimeter drainage. The apron cut of about 410 mm also stays under the 500 mm that would trigger a site reclassification.
  • The no-dig approach to paving is mandatory, not just prudent. Clause 6.6.3 is explicit: above existing grade, no excavation, no compaction.
  • A new drainage line through the pear's zone would need the plan amended. Clause 6.5.2 rules out additional services through a zone unless specified, which is why the sleeves cast into the garage slab are the recommended route out of the back garden: no tree approval, no supervision, and no risk of meeting a root you are not allowed to cut halfway along a trench. A hand-excavated or bored line through the zone is the fallback, with the plan amended first.

One inconsistency to raise with the arborist. The general notes on the tree protection drawing give a minimum bored depth of 700 mm for services, while clause 6.5.1 says 1,000 mm. Use the stricter figure unless he confirms otherwise. It matters for the stormwater outlet across the street tree's zone, where boring at either depth would put the invert below the kerb, so that crossing has to be hand or hydro excavated, which 6.5.1 expressly allows.

Also worth checking: mature eucalypts stand within a few metres of the rear fence, on reserve land. If they are protected public trees, their protection zones extend across the rear boundary and constrain digging there, including the corner swale.

Soil during the buildThe half of the back garden the tree plan does not cover

Yes, there is something to do, and the window for it is now rather than at handover. The tree management plan protects the soil properly — but only inside the fenced protection zones, and those cover the half of the back garden you are least going to grow in. Everything productive sits in the other half, where nothing protects the ground unless you ask for it.

What you actually have

Both boreholes found the same thing at the top: 100 mm of topsoil, described as silty sand, brown, moist, loose. That is the entire growing medium on this block. Below it is subsoil.

DepthBH1BH2
0 to 0.1 mSilty sand, loose — topsoilSilty sand, loose — topsoil
0.1 to 0.4 mGravelly clayey sand, medium dense to dense, dry, to 0.7 mClayey sand, loose to medium dense, moist
0.4 to 0.8 mSandy clay, medium to high plasticity, very stiff
0.7 to 1.1 mClayey sand, dense, dryGravelly sandy clay, very stiff to hard, to 1.0 m
Refusal1.1 m1.0 m

Two things follow. A hundred millimetres is thin enough that a single pass of a bobcat blade removes all of it, and thin enough that if it is mixed into the spoil heap it is gone — you cannot separate it again. And loose silty sand is both the most compactible and the most erodible material on the site, so it responds badly to everything a building site does.

The tree plan protects the wrong half

Protection zones cover just over half the open back garden, and the tree plan is strict inside them: no machinery without the arborist, no storage of materials or equipment, no trenching, levels maintained, ground protection where fencing is impractical, and beds later built above existing grade with no compaction of it. That is a good standard. Here is where the planned elements actually fall.

ElementProtected by the tree plan?
Mulched woodland bed, gravel path, lawn, gym matYes — inside the gum and pear zones
All three raised vegetable bedsNo
Firepit and its terraceNo
Both sheds, and the water tankNo
Paved terrace and outdoor kitchenNo

The productive strip on the east-north-east side is the sunniest ground on the block at 8.1 hours in summer, it is where the vegetables and fruit go, and it has no protection at all. It is also flat, open, close to the house and next to the access — which is to say it is exactly where a builder will stack bricks and turn a vehicle.

Compaction is the one you cannot undo. Loose sand compacts in a handful of passes, and the fix is mechanical ripping. Inside the protection zones ripping is forbidden. Outside them you are hand-digging, and hand tools will not lift compaction across a whole strip. So this is not a thing to repair later at some cost — for the way you are building this garden, it is close to permanent. Everything else in this section is recoverable. This one is not.

Most of it is already the builder's legal duty

Under the Environment Protection Act and Regulation the builder, not you, is responsible for having pollution controls in place before work starts and maintaining them until the site is stabilised. An erosion and sediment control plan is part of that. It requires sediment fencing, a single stabilised entry at least 3 m wide with aggregate over geotextile, stockpiles behind the sediment fence and under 2 m high, a contained washout area for concrete and render away from any drain, and downpipes connected early rather than at the end. On-the-spot fines run to $200 for an individual and $1,000 for a company, and serious offences reach $81,000.

So the conversation is not a favour to ask. It is: show me the erosion and sediment control plan, and let us agree the locations it names. The plan will exist; whether it puts the stockpile and the washout in the right corner of this particular block is the part worth your attention.

Four things specific to this block

  1. Put the damage where the paving is going. The strip between the house and the terrace line becomes hardstand anyway, and the existing driveway is already the nominated access. Stockpiles, the washout pit, material storage and vehicle turning all belong there. Ask for it in writing before the first delivery, because the default is wherever the first truck stops.
  2. The topsoil off the rear addition is being kept in its own pile, which is the single most valuable thing you can do here. The footings have to be founded below the topsoil, so it comes off regardless; the only question is whether it survives as soil or disappears into the spoil. What makes the difference is below.
  3. Nominate the washout, and keep it away from the native beds. Concrete, render and brick-cutting slurry are strongly alkaline, and the lime does not wash out of sandy soil in a hurry. Most of your shortlist — the grevilleas, banksias and hakeas — wants acid, low-phosphorus ground and is the least forgiving of a pH shift. A washout pit is required to be contained and away from drains regardless; the extra ask is that it is not sited on ground you intend to plant into.
  4. Keep everything off the reserve side. The tubestock planted behind the fence at Easter 2025 has taken, and the logs and mulch across that slope are doing erosion work the drainage design relies on. The tree plan already restricts access through unleased land to the identified points. Make the rear boundary a no-go for access, storage and spoil, and say so at the start rather than after a load of fill has been tipped over the fence.

Making the topsoil pile worth having

The rear addition footprint is 40 m². At 100 mm that is 4 cubic metres in the ground, about 5 loose — which is not a token amount. It is enough to fill all three raised vegetable beds to 400 mm, or to spread 100 mm over 40 m² of new bed. As a base for the productive garden, blended with compost, it beats anything delivered on a truck, because it is the soil the plants here already grow in.

FootprintAreaTopsoil at 100 mm
Rear addition40.0 m²4.0 m³
Garage44.9 m²4.5 m³
Link and kitchen addition14.9 m²1.5 m³
All the new work99.8 m²10.0 m³

The garage is the bigger area, and the same ask doubles the pile. Rear addition and garage together give 8.5 m³ — enough to fill the vegetable beds twice over, or to lift the whole productive strip. It is the same instruction to the same machine on the same day, so it costs nothing to extend.

Five things decide whether the pile is still soil in a year.

  • Topsoil only. The excavation goes well past 100 mm into clayey sand and sandy clay, and that subsoil is the bulk of the spoil. One pile with everything in it is a heap of fill, not a topsoil stockpile. This is the instruction most likely to be lost in translation on the day.
  • Low. Under two metres is the ACT requirement, and lower is better — a deep pile goes airless in the middle and the biology that makes topsoil worth saving dies there. At 4 m³ a pile a metre high needs about 12 m², which fits easily on ground that is going under paving anyway.
  • Seeded, not just left. This pile will sit until after handover, well past six months. Bare loose sand for that long erodes and becomes a weed seed bank. A cheap cover crop or even lawn seed over it holds it together and keeps it alive.
  • Behind the sediment fence, away from the washout, and out of the protection zones. Storage over a protection zone is forbidden by the tree plan in any case.
  • Not where it dams water. A pile on the uphill side of the addition does exactly what the diversion bund is being built to prevent.

Photograph the ground before they start. Walk the block and take dated photographs of the side strip, the rear corner and the reserve edge, with something in frame for scale. It costs ten minutes, it settles any later argument about what was already damaged, and it gives you a baseline to compare against at handover.

The moisture side of it

The Class P classification assumes normal moisture conditions and that the trees stay. The report is explicit that earthworks cutting deeper than 0.5 m or filling thicker than 0.4 m, or anything else causing abnormal moisture conditions near the building envelope, means the classification must be reassessed. During the build that means the same failures as the finished state, arriving early: a spoil heap damming water against the addition wall, a temporary downpipe discharging at ground level for six months, or a trench left open through a wet spell. Each is worth a look after the first heavy rain rather than at the end.

At handover

Before designing any bed, push a probe or a crowbar into the side strip in a few places and compare it against ground that was fenced off. If it goes in easily, you have kept your soil. If it stops dead in the top 200 mm, plan on building beds above the existing grade rather than digging into it — which is what the tree plan already requires inside the protection zones, and is the safe default across the whole back garden here.

Drainage designThe two lines, the numbers, and the route out

The block falls 2.08 m from the rear boundary to the street at about 1 in 19, so there is ample fall. The constraint is that the back garden is ringed by the protection zones of trees 1 and 2 where no trenching is allowed, and the addition, link and garage together enclose the rear pocket. There is no buried route from the back garden to the street that avoids both a protection zone and a building.

The route out is the garage

Two DN100 sleeves cast under the garage slab — one from the rear pocket, one from the enclosed courtyard — run to the driveway entirely clear of every protection zone, and neither passes under the link. From there they reach the kerb through the existing crossover at the north-east corner, the only part of the verge outside the street trees' zones. Invert 610.01 at the boundary against a kerb at 609.85, a fall of 1 in 50 across the verge, so it works by gravity. Both cost very little while the slab is being formed and become a serious problem afterwards.

The subsoil drain behind the retained edge needs an outlet, and none is shown. The engineer's 100 mm agricultural pipe collects the water moving sideways through the soil above the addition. If it is not piped away it simply discharges into the ground beside the footings, which is the problem it was meant to solve. It has to be connected, and the sleeve under the garage slab is the only route clear of the tree protection zones. Add it to the same trench.

The side strip does the rest

A DN150 spine runs the length of the block 2.5 m off the side boundary, clear of every zone, picking up the rear half of the house roof, the paving and the paths. It carries 5.3 litres a second in the design storm against a capacity of 45. Its outlet crosses tree 5's zone, so the last few metres must be hand or hydro excavated with the arborist present rather than bored — at the depth a bore requires, the invert would land below the kerb and could not discharge. Better still, find out whether the house already has a kerb outlet and reuse it.

The numbers

Earth shapingThe corner swale, the mulch blanket and the bund

Three pieces do the work of keeping reserve water away from the addition, and they are not interchangeable.

The corner swale — the only part that can be dug

The rear boundary falls 133 mm from the southern corner toward the west-south-west corner, about 1 in 164, so water running along the reserve path tends to arrive at that western corner by itself. That corner is also the only stretch of the rear boundary far enough from the gum to sit outside its protection zone, so it is the only part you can excavate.

The gum's trunk stands only 1.97 m from the rear boundary, and its structural root zone — the inner circle where nothing may be excavated, not even by hand — has a radius of 2.8 m, so it crosses the boundary by 830 mm. A channel following that boundary would pass within about 1.2 m of the trunk, which is why the swale is confined to the corner.

Positionwestern 4 m of the rear boundary, 0.8 to 1.2 m inside the fence
Distance from the gum7.1 m, clear of the 6.5 m protection zone
Cross-sectionabout 2 m wide, 250 mm deep, batters around 1 in 6
Gradearound 1 in 40, by cutting deeper toward the pit
Capacity294 L/s at 0.78 m/s
Outfallpit, then the sleeve under the garage slab to the street

294 litres a second is far more than this corner sees in ordinary rain, where the numbers are single digits. It is generous because the case worth designing for is the reserve bank overtopping. At 0.78 m/s it sits below the roughly 1.2 m/s at which grassed sandy soil begins to move, so it will not cut deeper once grass and sedges establish.

Two details matter more than the dimensions. Line the upstream end with rock, generously, because concentrated flow off the path arrives there with energy. And put a silt trap in the pit — a sump below the outlet with a removable grate — because a channel collecting hillside runoff brings sand and leaf litter, and shovelling that from a sump once a year is far easier than clearing it from the pipe under the garage.

The mulch blanket — what works across the middle

For the twelve or so metres of boundary in front of the gum there is no channel and cannot be one. Water crosses there and spreads as a thin sheet, as it does now. What handles it is the 100 mm layer of coarse woodchip the tree plan already requires. Coarse chip over sandy soil absorbs a surprising volume, and more importantly spreads flow and slows it rather than letting it collect into rivulets. Use coarse grade, around 25 mm, not fine or shredded — fine mulch floats. Lay logs or rock across the slope in the steeper pockets, as the reserve revegetation has done on the other side of the fence.

The diversion bund above the addition

A low ridge a few metres uphill of the addition's rear wall, angled so sheet flow crossing the woodland floor is turned aside into the side strip rather than continuing into the wall. It sits inside both trees' protection zones, so it is built up rather than dug: 100 mm of added material maximum, hand placed, arborist supervising. Build it from coarse woodchip rather than soil — 100 mm of clay or topsoil over a mature gum's root plate reduces the air reaching the roots, which is the reason the 100 mm cap exists. Make it wide and rounded rather than a sharp berm, so it overtops evenly along its length instead of breaching at one point.

How the three work together

In ordinary rain the mulch absorbs most of what crosses the boundary and the corner swale takes whatever concentrates at the western end. In heavier rain, sheet flow crosses the woodland floor, meets the bund, and is turned into the side strip where the overland path carries it to the street. In an extreme event the swale overtops as well and joins the same route. Nothing here holds water back; it all moves water past the building in a controlled way.

Sequence. Shape the corner swale, then build the bund, then mulch, then let a full wet season pass before planting around them, so the shaping can be corrected while it is still easy. Afterwards: clear the silt sump annually before winter, top up mulch every second or third year, and check after any severe storm that the bund has not been breached at a point.

The courtyardHot in summer, no natural outlet, everything in pots

The space between the rear addition, the link, the garage and the existing house needs handling on its own terms. It is a gated side courtyard about 4.06 m by 3.46 m — 14 square metres — with a covered stepping-stone path along the existing house wall and gates at the garage end. Walls are 2.4 to 2.8 m, and the ground sits 139 mm below the floor level of the rooms around it.

Bright for a courtyard, hot in summer, dark in winter

There is no canopy over this space, so what reaches it is whatever the surrounding walls let through.

Direct sun, hours per daySummerEquinoxWinter
Courtyard5.7 h3.1 h0.0 h
Open back garden, for comparison5.8 h4.4 h2.2 h

In summer that is nearly as much sun as the open garden, delivered into a still, walled enclosure with a black wall facing it, so the heat builds and does not blow away. Winter is the opposite: the surrounding walls block the low sun entirely, and midwinter returns nothing at all. Plan for a space that swings between the two rather than one with a settled light level.

The awning is the reliable position. The stepping-stone path along the existing house wall is roofed, so it stays shaded and sheltered year round while the open part of the courtyard takes the full summer load. Anything that wants steady conditions goes under the awning; anything in the open needs to be movable, which means a pot rather than the ground.

Do not plant a tree in the ground here. The site is a problem site precisely because trees near the footings dry the soil, and this position is against the house in reactive clay. Overhead shade should come from a structure, by extending the awning or adding a light sail, or from a large specimen in a pot. Avoid anything that scorches in hot, dry, reflected heat — a Japanese maple is the classic mistake in a courtyard like this one.

No fire in here

It is a tempting room for it — sheltered, walled, already the mildest outdoor spot on the property. It does not work, and the reasons stack up rather than balancing out.

Why notDetail
The clearance rule cannot be metAny open air fire needs three metres clear of anything that burns. The courtyard is 3.46 m wide, so a fire in the middle has 1.7 m to each wall
The smoke has nowhere to goEnclosed on four sides by walls 2.4 to 2.8 m, with half the sky visible and no wind. Smoke pools and comes back in through the doors, and rooms surround it on every side
Ash goes into the one drainThe courtyard has no natural outlet and a single channel grate. A blocked grate puts water into the bedrooms in under an hour
It cooks the plantingThe scheme here is ferns, staghorn and bromeliads in pots. Radiant heat at 1.7 m ends that
Carbon monoxideCombustion in a poorly ventilated enclosure with occupied rooms around it is the one risk on this list that is not merely expensive

What works instead: an electric radiant heater under the awning. No combustion, no smoke, no ash, no clearance problem, and it can stay out year round. The courtyard is already several degrees milder than anywhere else on a frosty night, so a modest heater turns it into a genuine winter sitting spot — which is what the fire was for. The fire itself belongs on the paved terrace, where the surround is non-combustible and there is room to sit around it.

Why it is the warmest spot on the block

Frost forms when the ground radiates heat to a clear night sky. A courtyard seeing about half the sky loses heat at roughly half that rate, the walls give back stored daytime warmth, and the wall on the northern side has heated rooms behind it. This will be the mildest outdoor position on the property on a frosty night, probably by several degrees, and that is what makes the rainforest planting realistic in Canberra at all.

What the materials mean

  • The existing house wall is blonde brick, and it is the wall the covered path runs along. It is the most reflective surface in the courtyard, faces away from the sun so stays cool, and has heated house behind it. The best wall in the space by every measure, and the one to mount things on.
  • The addition and link walls are black Axon. The addition's wall faces the sun, so it will be the hottest surface on a summer afternoon, radiating heat even with the ground shaded. Keep pots off it and away from its base. Dark cladding reflects almost nothing, so it contributes no useful light.

Planting: everything in pots

Pots solve three problems at once. The soil here is reactive clay right against the footings. And a rain-shadowed courtyard needs regular watering, which is exactly what you cannot do to soil beside footings. In pots on the paving, water drains onto the paving and into the courtyard drain, so you can water freely and none of it reaches the ground beside the footings.

PositionConditionsPlants
Blonde brick wall, above the stepping stones, under the awningThe most sheltered position, shaded from summer sun and protected overhead from frost and rain, and the path gives access at working heightStag horn and elk horn mounted here. The only position on the property where they have a real chance
Ground level, in pots, off the black wallsSeveral hours of direct summer sun, almost none in winterTree fern, bird's nest fern, hardy ground ferns, burawang. All tolerate Canberra frost once established, but none will take the full summer load here. Keep them where the walls shade them through the middle of the day, or move them under the awning over summer — which is why they are in pots
Between the stepping stonesTrafficked, shaded, no soil depth neededDichondra or moss in the joints for softness underfoot

Bromeliads suit this space, wanting bright indirect light rather than either deep shade or direct sun; keep them out of the worst of the afternoon. Group the pots rather than spreading them out, which raises local humidity and makes hand watering quicker, and keep plants spaced and off the walls, because still humid air in a shaded enclosure encourages fungal problems.

Drainage: there is no natural way out

The courtyard is enclosed on all four sides and sits below the floor level around it, so water landing in it cannot run anywhere. The floor plan already shows a 1200 mm strip drain at the ensuite threshold, so the need for an outlet is recognised; the question is where it goes. Its own runoff is small: 0.66 litres a second in a one-in-a-hundred-year burst, about 640 litres over an hour. Capacity is not the issue. Having an outlet is.

A soakage pit is the wrong answer. Soaking water into reactive clay a metre or two from footings is what both the geotechnical report and the CSIRO guidance warn against. It has to be piped.

The route is a sleeve under the garage slab. The ground falls toward the existing house wall, so the natural low line is along the base of that wall beside the stepping stones, which is also where a channel grate belongs to catch wall and path run-off. From the northern end of that channel a short pipe runs under the garage slab to join the line from the rear pocket. Nothing passes under the link. About 2.6 m of sleeve, with the levels working comfortably at roughly 1 in 17.

There is no downpipe in the courtyard on the current drawings, and it should stay that way. The courtyard holds about 1.9 cubic metres before water reaches the doors, so with no roof water a blocked grate takes about 48 minutes to get there. Add 20 square metres of roof and it is 19 minutes; add 40 and it is 11. That is the difference between a nuisance you notice and water in the bedrooms.

Even so, leaf litter blows in and collects against the walls with no wind to clear it, so keep the redundancy: a long channel grate along the wall rather than a single square grate so partial blockage still leaves capacity, a litter sump below the outlet where you can reach it, and a second pipe laid in the same sleeve trench while it is open.

Clearing the grate is routine rather than optional, particularly through autumn. It is the one piece of maintenance in this garden where skipping a year has consequences inside the house.

To settle before the slab goes down

  1. Where the ensuite strip drain discharges, and confirmation that no downpipe is added into the courtyard later.
  2. Both sleeves under the garage slab, plus a spare pipe in the courtyard trench.
  3. The garage roof: fall direction, gutter position, and the number and location of downpipes, given it takes the house roof as well.
  4. Paving level against the damp-proof course. The courtyard floor is only 139 mm below the room floors, and paving normally wants at least 150 mm below the damp-proof course. If it has to go lower, that is excavation next to footings in reactive clay and the engineer should specify how.

Access is already resolved: the gates at the garage end and the stepping-stone path give a way in, wide enough to carry a potted plant through.

Paved terrace and the terracingOne wall, how much step it can hold, and what sits either side

Two constraints shape where the paving and the kitchen can go, even with exact positions unresolved.

  • Paving inside a tree protection zone has to be built up, not cut in. Clause 6.6.3 of the tree plan requires paths and beds inside a zone to sit above existing grade with no excavation and no compaction, so a conventional excavated base course is not available there. The permitted build-ups are cellular geotextile, or rumble boards over 200 mm of coarse woodchip, or rated mats. They work but are awkward to finish neatly under paving, so it is simpler to keep the paved area clear of the zone.
  • The kitchen needs water, waste, power and probably gas. Services through a zone need hand or hydro excavation, or boring at 1,000 mm, and clause 6.5.2 rules out additional services through a zone unless the plan specifies them. Siting the kitchen in the band clear of tree 2's zone avoids the question entirely.

The band from about 16.7 m to 19.9 m off the rear boundary, alongside the kitchen addition, is clear of every protection zone and adjoins the existing patio and its awning. A 3.2 by 3.0 m area there takes the kitchen with no tree constraint and the shortest service runs. The paved terrace sits at 17.6 m so it is also clear; widening it westward means building up rather than cutting in.

Sun there is 11.0 hours in December, 3.9 at the equinox and effectively none in June, so treat it as a warm-weather space and put any winter sitting position in the rear pocket instead. Grade the paving to fall away from the house at 1:60 minimum, and connect the sink waste properly rather than letting it soak beside a footing.

The terrace, and how much step is available

The back garden falls 0.92 m from the rear boundary to the house, about 1 in 19. That is the entire budget for a level change, and it is spread over twenty metres, so a step between two levels has to be manufactured rather than found. Between the lawn and the paving the natural fall is only about 0.2 m.

The limit is the geotechnical trigger: cut deeper than 0.5 m or fill thicker than 0.4 m and the site classification has to be reassessed. Fill is the binding one, because a raised lawn is fill at its downhill edge.

Lawn platform at RL 611.90ValueAgainst the limit
Cut at the uphill end0.12 mwell inside 0.5 m
Fill at the wall0.38 mjust inside 0.4 m
Wall height, paving at RL 611.500.40 m0.45 m if the paving drops 50 mm

So the honest answer on height is about 400 mm, and 450 at a stretch — the bottom of the range rather than the middle of it. A metre is not available: it would need roughly 0.6 m of fill behind the wall, half again over the trigger, and the reassessment that follows is a cost and a delay on a site that is already Class P. Four hundred is a comfortable perch and it reads as a proper edge to the paved room, which is most of what a terrace is for.

Where the wall can go

Not far, and this is the real constraint rather than the height. Tree protection zones cover just over half the open back garden, and inside them levels must be maintained and nothing may be dug. A wall needs a footing, so it has to sit outside them entirely. Running down the paving's uphill edge, the clear ground runs out about 3.2 m from the east-north-east boundary, where the pear's zone begins.

The wall is a two metre run, not a garden-wide terrace. It holds the lawn's downhill edge and gives the paving a back to it. Beyond that the ground stays as it is, which is no bad thing — a single short wall reads as deliberate, where a long one crossing the whole garden would have been unbuildable.

The lawn, and the thing it collides with

A level platform of about 20 m² works: roughly 9.8 m along the slope by 2 m wide, sitting on the clear ground between the boundary and the pear's protection zone. Big enough for a toddler, small enough to be honest about.

It sits on the overland flow path, and that has to be solved before anything is built. The east-north-east strip is the route reserve water takes to the street if the raised path behind the fence ever overtops — 236 litres a second, and the only gravity escape there is. A raised lawn platform across it is a dam. The flow has to be given a formed route along the boundary fence instead, and at the width available it runs at about 1.6 m/s, which is faster than grass alone holds. That means a rock-lined or turf-reinforced channel rather than a grassed swale, and it is a change to the drainage design, so it needs the stormwater contractor to price it and the levels checked before the wall goes in.

The steps from the lawn down to the paving belong at the boundary end, on the flow line, built broad and armoured. In normal use they are the way down; in the rare event they are the spillway. That is the neatest resolution available, and it costs nothing extra if it is designed in from the start.

What goes where now

AreaUse
Paved terrace, against the houseOutdoor kitchen, seating, the firepit, and the planters. Non-combustible, level, and where people actually gather
Raised lawn, east-north-east stripAbout 20 m² of level grass, one step up from the paving
Upslope of the lawnFruit trees, espaliered along the boundary fence where the strip is too narrow for open forms
Under the gum and pearDry-shade woodland on existing grade. Nothing dug, nothing levelled
Rear pocket, west of the additionUtility: bikes, bins, sheds, tank and clothesline. 60 m² usable, of which the built items take about 14

Vegetables move into planters on the paving rather than beds in the ground. Tomatoes, herbs and berries all do well in large pots, they sit at the kitchen where they get used, they need no soil disturbance and no protection zone permission, and they are the obvious home for the topsoil coming off the rear addition. Blueberries in particular prefer a pot, because they want acid soil this block does not have.

PlantingZone by zone, working outward from the house

Two rules organise most of it.

The closer to the house, the less water a plant should need. Lawn or dry-tolerant groundcover beside the paving, then progressively thirstier plants, shrubs and finally trees as you move away. The reason is the clay beside the house, which swells and shrinks with moisture; keeping it at a steady moisture level protects the footings, and the way to do that is not to put anything demanding near them.

Inside a tree protection zone, build up rather than dig down. Beds sit on the existing ground, planting holes are dug by hand, and nothing is excavated or compacted.

Colour key for the planting layer

Turn on the Planting zones layer on the interactive plan to see these in position.

ZoneApproach
