Front: structural and screeningShadiest half of the block, 4.3 h summer down to 2.3 h in winter. Sun-lovers in the canopy gaps, shade-tolerant natives beneath. Screening at 1.5 to 2.5 m. Plant through mulch, never excavate.

The paved apron, and the first three metres

A 900 mm band of paving right around the house, sloping away at 1 in 60 or better. No beds, no plants, no irrigation, no taps inside it. This is the buffer that keeps building moisture stable and stops splash and soil contact with the walls.

From the apron out to about three metres you are still in the ground that affects the footings. Dry-tolerant groundcovers and low grasses here — Scleranthus, Dichondra, Poa, Lomandra — which take a dry summer without help. If you run drip, run it on a tap you turn off, not a timer. Avoid aggressive root systems and anything you will feel obliged to water twice a week.

The sunny strip along the east-north-east boundary

The best summer growing ground on the property at 8.1 hours, and 4.0 at the winter solstice, spread fairly evenly across the day. Sandy and free draining, and four metres or more clear of the house, so you can water it properly without consequence for the footings.

Raised vegetable beds, fruit espaliered flat against the fence to use the vertical space and reflected warmth, and citrus in the sunniest section. The fence itself costs about an hour a day, so anything low and light-hungry does better a metre or two out from it than hard against it.

Under the two big trees

One to four hours of sun, dry soil, and constant root competition from a mature gum and the pear. The hardest planting on the site and the least forgiving of impatience. Turf will not hold, and neither will anything wanting regular water.

Spread 100 mm of coarse woodchip, which the tree plan requires anyway, and plant small tubestock through it into hand-dug holes, with beds built up on the surface rather than cut in. Bursaria, Correa, Rhagodia, Poa, Dianella and Lomandra all cope. Expect slow establishment and hand water through the first two summers, after which they look after themselves. This becomes the low-maintenance part of the garden once away.

The patch of lawn

Turf will fail under the trees and is not worth fighting. Dichondra repens is already on your must-have list, is shade tolerant, needs no soil build-up and is soft underfoot. That is the lawn, in the lighter pocket between the paving and the woodland.

The rear boundary and the swale

The wettest and most erodible ground on the block, and periodically running water. Planting here does structural work as much as visual: roots hold the soil and slow the flow.

Sedges and tussocks through the swale — Poa labillardierei, Ficinia nodosa, Carex. Behind them the acacia and hakea screen from your local provenance list, which gives the filtered privacy from the walking track and matches the revegetation on the reserve side of the fence. Plant this before the first winter if you can, because bare ground in a channel is what fails.

The rear pocket and firepit terrace

Afternoon and evening sun, free-draining sand, clear of the tree zones, so this is the one part of the back garden where you can dig freely. It is also the sunniest part of the back garden across the whole year, holding 4.5 hours in midwinter, which is wasted on a utility yard but hard to avoid given it is the only route to the rear — the paved terrace near the house drops to nothing in June.

The courtyard

The rainforest group, all in pots and mounted. See the courtyard section for positions.

The front garden

The shadier half of the block, because of the liquidambar and the two street ashes, and the part where you cannot change levels. Proteas, leucadendrons, grass trees and waratah need full sun and sharp drainage, so they go in the open gaps between canopies, not under them, with shade-tolerant natives beneath. Everything planted through mulch, nothing excavated. The screening layer for privacy sits just inside the front boundary at 1.5 to 2.5 metres mature height, covering the sunken lounge and bedroom windows without blocking their light.

The front garden: mounds, and why they suit this block

Mounding is the right instinct here, and not only for the look. You cannot dig this block: there is 100 mm of topsoil, the ground near the house is reactive clay the engineer is designing around, and 59 per cent of the front garden sits inside a tree protection zone where excavation is forbidden and beds have to be built above existing grade. Building up is the compliant way to get root depth, so the constraint and the aesthetic point the same way.

It also suits the planting. Most of the natives on your list that mind anything at all mind wet feet — the grevilleas, banksias and hakeas want sharp drainage, and a raised mound over free-draining sand gives them exactly that. And a mound is the obvious home for the topsoil coming off the build.

WhereMound heightWhy
Outside the protection zonesup to 400 mmFill thicker than 400 mm triggers a reclassification. 400 is ample for the effect
Inside a protection zone100 mmSame rule as the diversion bund — more than that starts cutting air to the roots
Within 0.9 m of the housenoneThe paved apron stays clear, and nothing may raise ground against the walls

Three placement rules, and the first is the one that shapes the whole front garden. The driveway takes the western strip. It runs from the garage door at 27.9 m out to the crossover at the street, about 2.7 m wide along the western boundary, and it is the sunniest ground in the front — which is simply not available. Everything plantable sits between it and the house, or in the strip on the far side. Second, keep mounds off the overland flow corridor along the east-north-east boundary; a 400 mm mound sitting on it is a dam, the same problem the raised lawn creates out the back. Third, keep them clear of the east wing, which reaches further into the front garden than it looks on a plan. Set them as long, low, overlapping swells rather than discrete humps, running with the fall rather than across it so they do not dam water on its way to the street. Layer the planting by height rather than by species block: prostrate things on the crowns where it is driest, the mid layer on the flanks, and the structural plants in the hollows between where water gathers.

Fruit trees in the front — one or two, chosen for form

The instinct is reasonable but the numbers are against most of it. The front garden averages 4.3 hours of summer sun against 8.1 in the side strip out the back, because the liquidambar and the two street ashes put 35 per cent of it under canopy in exactly the season fruit needs light. Only 41 per cent of it is outside a protection zone. And your list is almost entirely deciduous, so it is bare through winter — which is when the low sun and the bare street make privacy matter most, and the ashes and liquidambar are bare too. Fruit trees are the wrong tool for the sense of entry and the screening.

TreeVerdict
QuinceYes. The best of the six for here — very frost hardy, gnarled cottage form, blossom worth the space, and a cooking fruit so a modest crop is no loss. It goes in the band between the house and the driveway, which at 7.3 hours is the sunniest planting ground the front has, and 5.5 m off the house wall
PomegranateYes. 3 m, frost hardy once established, ornamental for months. It needs heat to ripen, so it goes in the east-north-east corner beyond the liquidambar canopy rather than under it, where it also gets the reflected warmth off the east wing
FigNot the front. 5 m of spread and roots that go looking for water, and the front stormwater line runs through it. A fig beside that pipe is a problem you would not see coming
CherrySkip, or accept it as ornamental. The biggest of the six, most sweet varieties need a pollinator, birds take the crop, and 4.3 hours will not ripen it well
LemonA pot on the back terrace instead. That is the warmest, most sheltered spot on the property at 11.0 hours in summer, and a pot can be moved under cover in a hard frost. Citrus in Canberra wants a warm wall, not an open front garden
Dwarf mulberryFine at 2.5 m, but keep it well away from the entry path, the paving and the car. The fruit stains, and the birds spread it further than the canopy

The plan tool opens with the driveway drawn and four mounds and both trees placed clear of it. All four sit inside the liquidambar or street ash protection zones, so all four are the 100 mm sort — the ground outside those zones in the front is almost entirely driveway. Select any of them and the panel confirms it, along with the sun: the band between the house and the driveway returns 7.3 hours in summer against the front garden average of 4.3, which is why the quince is there.

Two in the front, the rest out the back or in pots. Quince and pomegranate earn their place on form as much as fruit, which is the cottage logic. The productive trees belong in the side strip where the sun is, espaliered along the boundary fence because the strip is too narrow for open forms — and espalier gives you more trees in less space, which is the answer to wanting five of them.

Everything else native from here is straightforward, because the list already is. The cottage effect comes from layering heights and repeating a few things often, not from variety: prostrate grevillea, scleranthus and pigface on the crowns; correa, dianella and lomandra through the middle; banksia, bursaria, hakea and callistemon for structure; and a dwarf eucalypt or two for the canopy the front will want once the ashes eventually go.

Two things to avoid. Do not run automatic irrigation inside the apron zone or against the walls; overwatering on a timer is one of the most common causes of footing damage and is entirely avoidable. And do not plant a new large tree close to the house — the site is already a problem site because of tree-induced soil drying, and another one compounds the issue the engineer is designing around.

Design the planInteractive: drag, resize, plant, and see sun, levels, cut and cost as you go

A working design tool rather than a diagram. Drag anything to move it, grab the corner handle to resize, the arm to rotate. Add hard elements from the library, place plants from your own list at their mature spread, and delete or duplicate whatever you select. Scroll to zoom, drag the background to pan, and everything snaps to 50 mm and stays true to scale.

The Selected panel below the plan is the point of it. Select anything and it tells you four things about that exact position: how much sun it gets in summer, at the equinox and in midwinter, computed from the same model as the solar study; the ground level from the surveyed contours; how much cut and fill levelling it would take, and whether that breaches the half-metre cut or 400 mm fill that would trigger a site reclassification; and what the tree plan permits there, naming the method rather than just flagging a problem.

Beside it, running quantities and cost against the $10,000 budget, so you can see what a decision costs before making it. Rates are indicative, for materials with you doing the labour, and exclude the stormwater contractor.

Try this. Place a fig from the palette in the sunny side strip, then drag it under the two big trees and watch the sun figure collapse from about eleven hours to under two. That is the difference the position makes, and it is why the productive garden goes where it does.

Green in the panel means clear. Amber means it can be built there, but only with the method named. Red is a hard clash — a structural root zone, a building, or the boundary.
